what_it_does: Controlling a large quantum computer requires many separate control boards working in tight coordination — some gates require two boards to fire signals within nanoseconds of each other. Existing systems either broadcast every decision to all controllers (wasteful) or stall and wait for a reply signal each time synchronisation is needed (slow). Distributed-HISQ introduces a hardware instruction set that decouples the control language from the underlying electronics, and a pre-booking synchronisation protocol that can eliminate waiting overhead entirely when there is enough deterministic work happening beforehand, reducing average execution time by 22.8% and cutting error rates by roughly 5x.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Quantum gates have a fixed, known duration. If controller A knows it will finish its own work at time T, it can send a synchronisation message in advance — booking a meeting — rather than waiting until the last moment and then stalling until the reply arrives. As long as the message round-trip completes before time T, there is zero wasted time.

HISQ — the instruction set. The hardware instruction set for quantum computing (HISQ) is built as an extension to the standard RISC-V 32I instruction set used in ordinary embedded processors. Rather than naming quantum operations ('apply an X gate to qubit 3'), which would require different hardware for every type of quantum chip, HISQ instructions say: 'send codeword W to output port P at time-point T.' The mapping from codeword to actual analog signal (a microwave pulse, a voltage ramp, etc.) is configured in hardware tables — the same digital microarchitecture can therefore drive superconducting qubits with fixed-frequency transmons or with tunable couplers, without changing the instruction set. Validation on a real 66-qubit chip showed the same HISQ core controlling both the signal-generation boards and the measurement boards, with the same instruction triggering an X gate on one board and a readout on the other.

BISP — the synchronisation protocol. When two adjacent controllers need to synchronise, each sends a 1-bit signal and simultaneously starts counting for N cycles (N equals the known wire-delay between boards). Synchronisation completes when two conditions are both true: (1) the N-cycle count finishes, and (2) the matching signal from the neighbour has arrived. If the signal arrives early, the controller keeps running with no pause. If it arrives late, the controller stalls only for the gap — never longer. For region-level synchronisation across many controllers, a router collects the earliest-ready times from all controllers, broadcasts the latest of them, and all controllers resume together. The hardware cost is only 13 look-up-table cells (LUTs) per synchronisation unit on an FPGA.

Network topology. The system uses a balanced tree of routers for region-wide synchronisation (minimising the number of network hops) and a mesh of direct links between neighbouring controllers — mirroring the physical layout of qubits on the chip — for the common case of two-qubit gates between adjacent qubits.

The result. Across benchmarks of dynamic quantum circuits and logical error-correcting circuits, BISP reduces average runtime by 22.8% and reduces computation errors by roughly 5x compared to the lock-step broadcast scheme used by IBM's quantum control system.
